meta.titre: Nutrient Cycling in Ecosystems: Gersmehl models, store sizes and conservation
meta.sous_theme: Nutrient stores and flows in biomes

sections.contenu_markdown: Walk into the rainforest of south west Cameroon and you meet tall trees, thick undergrowth and a forest floor that holds surprisingly little loose leaf matter. Yet farmers who clear such land for crops often find that yields fall after a few seasons. The explanation is the way nutrients are stored and moved within the ecosystem. Examiners ask you to recognise a biome from the sizes of its nutrient stores, to account for these sizes, and to advise on conservation. This course gives you the model, the reasoning and a method for the written answers.

items: An ecosystem is a community of living things together with its physical environment, linked by flows of energy and nutrients.
Biomass is the mass of living organisms, litter is dead plant material on the ground, and soil holds minerals and humus.
Decomposers such as bacteria and fungi break down dead organic matter and release nutrients.

sections.titre: Nutrient stores and transfers in the Gersmehl model
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Key terms
A **nutrient cycle** is the movement of mineral nutrients between the living and non-living parts of an ecosystem. Gersmehl's model shows three **stores**: **biomass** (living matter), **litter** (dead leaves and wood on the surface) and **soil** (humus and minerals). In the diagram, the size of a circle is proportional to the store and the thickness of an arrow to the rate of transfer. The nutrients move by **uptake** (soil to biomass through roots), **litterfall** (biomass to litter) and **decomposition** (litter to soil). **Inputs** include weathering of rock, rainfall and dust, and fertiliser; **losses** include leaching, runoff, erosion, harvesting and burning.

### Store sizes in some biomes
| Biome | Biomass | Litter | Soil | Main reasons |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tropical rainforest | Large | Small | Small | Heat and moisture speed up decomposition; heavy rain leaches the soil; roots take up nutrients quickly |
| Temperate grassland | Small | Small | Largest | Grasses die back each year and decay into thick humus; leaching is limited |
| Boreal forest (taiga) | Medium | Large | Small | Cold slows decomposition so dead needles build up |
| Desert | Small | Small | Small | Lack of water limits growth and decay |

### Why the rainforest is delicately balanced
The nutrient cycle is fast, so nutrients spend little time in litter or soil. Most of them are held in the living trees, and the forest feeds itself from its own dead leaves. If the biomass is removed by logging or burning, the store is lost, the thin litter store cannot replace it, and rain leaches the small soil store, so fertility falls within a few years.

### Management
Protect the biomass store and keep the cycle closed: protected areas such as Korup National Park, selective logging with replanting, agroforestry, long fallow in shifting cultivation, a ban on burning, mulching and cover crops, and community forests.

variantes.nom: Recognise the biome from the stores
variantes.quand_utiliser: When a question describes the sizes of the stores or the direction of the transfers.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Find the largest store first. A large biomass with small litter and soil points to a tropical rainforest; a dominant soil store points to a temperate grassland; a dominant litter store points to a boreal forest. Then use the arrows: strong transfers from biomass to litter and weak transfers from soil to biomass fit a cold or slow cycle.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked to account for variations between biomes or to propose conservation.
variantes.contenu_markdown: For variation, link climate to decomposition, leaching and uptake. For fragility, identify the largest store, explain why its loss cannot be repaired quickly, and name human activities that remove it. For strategies, name measures that match the store and say how each works.

sections.enonce_markdown:
The table gives invented nutrient stores, in kg per hectare, for two ecosystems P and Q.

| Ecosystem | Biomass | Litter | Soil |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | 1,200 | 60 | 240 |
| Q | 100 | 50 | 850 |

(a) Calculate the percentage of the total nutrients held in each store of P and Q. (b) Identify the biome of each. (c) Explain why the litter store of P is small. (d) Suggest one measure to protect P.

etapes.action: Calculate the totals and the percentages for P.
etapes.justification: A percentage is the store divided by the total, multiplied by 100.

etapes.action: Calculate the totals and the percentages for Q.
etapes.justification: The same method applies to the second ecosystem.
The pattern of the stores matches the model.
etapes.resultat_markdown: P has a very large biomass and small litter and soil stores, so it is a tropical rainforest. Q has a dominant soil store and small biomass and litter, so it is a temperate grassland.

etapes.action: Explain the small litter store of P.
etapes.justification: The explanation links climate to the speed of decomposition.
etapes.resultat_markdown: High temperature and constant moisture make decomposers very active, so fallen leaves rot within a short time and nutrients move quickly into the soil and are taken up by roots again.

etapes.action: Suggest a measure to protect P.
etapes.justification: The measure must protect the store that holds most nutrients.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Establish protected areas or practise selective logging with replanting, so the biomass store, with 80 per cent of the nutrients, is not removed.

sections.conclusion_markdown: P holds **80 per cent** of its nutrients in biomass, **4 per cent** in litter and **16 per cent** in soil, so it is a tropical rainforest. Q holds **10, 5 and 85 per cent** in biomass, litter and soil, so it is a temperate grassland. The litter in P is small because rapid decomposition and uptake keep the cycle fast, and protecting the biomass is the key to conserving P.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that rainforest soils are fertile because the vegetation is so lush.
items.pourquoi_faux: The lush vegetation shows a large biomass store, not a rich soil. The soil store of a rainforest is small because nutrients are leached and taken up quickly.
items.correction_markdown: State that most nutrients are held in the biomass and that the soil is poor once the trees are removed.

items.erreur_markdown: Claiming that the rainforest has a thick litter layer that stores most nutrients.
items.pourquoi_faux: Warm, wet conditions make decay very rapid, so litter does not accumulate. A thick litter store belongs to cold biomes such as the boreal forest.
items.correction_markdown: Describe the litter store of the rainforest as small and linked to fast decomposition.

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing the size of a store with the rate of a flow, for example saying a thick arrow means a large circle.
items.pourquoi_faux: In Gersmehl's diagram the circle shows how much is stored and the arrow shows how fast nutrients move. A small store can have a fast transfer.
items.correction_markdown: Read the circle for the store and the arrow for the transfer, and discuss them separately.

items.erreur_markdown: Describing the ecosystem as closed and ignoring inputs and losses.
items.pourquoi_faux: Ecosystems gain nutrients from rock weathering and rain, and lose them by leaching, runoff, erosion and harvesting. Ignoring these hides how people disturb the balance.
items.correction_markdown: Mention at least one input and one loss when you explain how the system works.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that burning the forest permanently adds nutrients to the soil.
items.pourquoi_faux: Ash gives a brief increase in fertility, but without the trees, heavy rain leaches the nutrients away and the soil store soon declines.
items.correction_markdown: Explain that burning gives a short-term gain followed by loss through leaching and erosion.

items.enonce_markdown: In an ecosystem, the nutrient stores are biomass 450 kg per hectare, litter 350 kg per hectare and soil 200 kg per hectare. (a) Calculate the percentage in each store. (b) Name the flow that moves nutrients from living plants to the litter, and the flow that moves them from litter to the soil.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Total $=450+350+200=1\,000$. Biomass **45 per cent**, litter **35 per cent**, soil **20 per cent**. (b) Biomass to litter is **litterfall**; litter to soil is **decomposition** (mineralisation).

items.enonce_markdown: A boreal forest has the following invented nutrient stores in kg per hectare: biomass 300, litter 600, soil 100. (a) Calculate the percentage in each store. (b) Explain why the litter store is the largest.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Total $=1\,000$, so biomass **30 per cent**, litter **60 per cent**, soil **10 per cent**. (b) Low temperatures slow decomposers, and needles are tough and acidic, so dead material decays slowly and accumulates on the surface. Little nutrient reaches the soil, so the soil store stays small. **Any two linked reasons carry full marks.**

items.enonce_markdown: A timber company plans to log a large block of tropical rainforest and then plant food crops. (a) Explain why the plan threatens the long-term fertility of the land. (b) Propose and justify two changes to the plan that would keep the nutrient cycle working.
items.solution_markdown: (a) Most nutrients are held in the trees. Logging removes the biomass store, so the nutrients leave with the timber; the small litter store cannot rebuild the soil; heavy rain leaches the thin soil and exposed ground erodes, so crop yields fall within a few years. (b) Award marks for two justified changes, for example: practise selective logging, leaving seed trees and canopy so that litterfall and uptake continue; keep strips of forest or practise agroforestry so tree roots and leaf fall continue to feed the soil; replant native species after cutting; leave long fallow periods before re-cropping. **Two justified changes carry full marks.**

items_markdown: Gersmehl's model has three stores (biomass, litter, soil) and three main transfers (uptake, litterfall, decomposition), with inputs and losses.
Tropical rainforest: large biomass, small litter and soil stores, because heat and rain make decay, leaching and uptake very fast.
Temperate grassland has a dominant soil store; the boreal forest has a dominant litter store because cold slows decomposition.
The rainforest biomass is the most fragile store: when it is removed, the nutrients go with it and the thin soil cannot replace them.
Conservation: protected areas, selective logging with replanting, agroforestry, long fallow, no burning and mulch or cover crops.
